结合目标浏览器判断特性支持，按指南为关键操作保留后备行为。

# Modern Web Guidance 使用说明

可从 [SKILL.md](../../demos/materials/modern-web-guidance/SKILL.md) 开始，按任务阅读快照中的 209 篇指南。上游的主题索引见 [README](../../demos/materials/modern-web-guidance/README.md)。

## 按任务检索

在 Node.js 22 或更新版本中，通过上游的命令行工具（CLI）搜索单个界面行为，再按搜索结果中的 `id` 读取指南。以导航抽屉为例。

```sh
npx modern-web-guidance@1.0.0 search "navigation drawer"
npx modern-web-guidance@1.0.0 retrieve "navigation-drawer"
```

选定做法后，查看指南列出的浏览器支持与后备方案。比如采用 View Transitions API 时，先检测 `document.startViewTransition`，不支持时仍执行原有的 DOM 更新。

## 官方示例

- 导航抽屉。打开抽屉，再用滑动、点击遮罩或按 Escape 关闭。 [原文指南](../../demos/materials/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-components/navigation-drawer.md) · [官方 Demo](https://mwg-demos.web.app/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/blob/544c250575f7811d87fef8b1c064bc9571cbfb80/guides/ui-components/navigation-drawer/demo.html)
- 容器尺寸与组件布局。拖动虚线框右下角，观察卡片在容器宽度跨过 400px 时由纵排切到横排。 [原文指南](../../demos/materials/modern-web-guidance/guides/css/size-aware-styling.md) · [官方 Demo](https://mwg-demos.web.app/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/blob/544c250575f7811d87fef8b1c064bc9571cbfb80/guides/css/size-aware-styling/demo.html)
- 同文档视图过渡。点开商品再返回，观察缩略图和标题在列表与详情之间的过渡。 [原文指南](../../demos/materials/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-behaviors/same-document-transitions.md) · [官方 Demo](https://mwg-demos.web.app/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/blob/544c250575f7811d87fef8b1c064bc9571cbfb80/guides/ui-behaviors/same-document-transitions/demo.html)

引用原文时保留署名与许可，出处见[许可说明](../../demos/materials/modern-web-guidance/LICENSES.md)。

# Modern Web Guidance · Web 平台指南 · 复用 Prompt

[结构化条目](../../entries/materials/modern-web-guidance.json)

先阅读 Modern Web Guidance 的 SKILL.md。把当前网页任务拆成单个界面行为或浏览器能力，检索并读取对应指南。结合项目的目标浏览器选择 HTML、CSS 或浏览器 API，按需做功能检测，为关键操作保留后备方案。完成后说明采用了哪些指南及对应实现。

## 制作约束

- 固定快照可直接阅读，命令行检索使用上游的 npm 包，要求 Node.js 22 或更新版本。
- 结合目标浏览器判断特性支持，按指南为关键操作保留后备行为。

# Modern Web Guidance [Modern Web Guidance](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform. *Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.* [Documentation](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) · [Eval Dashboard](https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/) · [Source Code](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src) · [Report an Issue](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/issues) ## Quickstart ```shell npx modern-web-guidance@latest install ``` This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See [Alternative Installation Methods](#-alternative-installation-methods) below. #### Try it out (without installing) ```shell # Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop" # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer" # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan . ``` ## Why? Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions. Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code. **Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap.** Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on: * **Modern Browser APIs**: Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. * **Performance & Accessibility**: Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. * **Responsible Fallbacks**: Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries. ## What's Included? We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are **designed to be token-efficient**; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know. ### Core Disciplines

🎨 User Experience

Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color).

📐 CSS Layout

Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid, modern color spaces like oklch, text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming).

⚡ Performance

Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield).

📝 Forms & UI

Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields).

♿ Accessibility

Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability).

🤖 Built-in AI

Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).
_View an example:_ [the `navigation-drawer` guide](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-components/navigation-drawer.md). #### The full list

### Safe Adoption of Modern Features * **Progressive Enhancement & Nuanced Fallbacks**: We distinguish between purely additive enhancements (like speculative preloading) which are safe to let older browsers silently ignore, and critical behaviors (like dialog controls or network beacons) where we write highly considered, low-overhead fallbacks. * **Responsible Fallbacks**: We prioritize lightweight, case-specific custom fallbacks (<50 LOC) or conditionally-loaded polyfills instead of heavy third-party bundles. * **Gotchas & Quirks**: We document hidden platform limitations, such as the 64KB payload quota for `fetchLater()` or macOS-specific scrollbar behaviors. * **Baseline-Aware Integration**: We leverage real-time compatibility data from the **Baseline** project so agents dynamically adapt to current browser support. * **Origin Trial & Volatile Feature Gates**: Guides covering experimental **Origin Trial** APIs or **volatile features** (single-engine features shipped within the last 3 months or still stabilizing) remain discoverable via `search`, but are gated on `retrieve` so agents do not adopt unstable APIs without explicit developer consent. ### Project Configuration (`.mwgrc`) Configure Origin Trial and volatile feature opt-ins for a repository with an optional `.mwgrc` JSON file in your project root (or `~/.mwgrc` as a user-level fallback), which you can commit to share across your team: | CLI Command | `.mwgrc` Key | Effect | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-origin-trials` | `"allowOriginTrials": true` | Unlocks guides for experimental Origin Trial APIs. | | `npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-volatile-features` | `"allowVolatileFeatures": true` | Unlocks guides for volatile single-engine features. | ## How It Works 1. **Activation**: The coding agent activates the `modern-web-guidance` skill because of a relevant task. # Modern Web Guidance

Search and retrieve standardized modern web best practices at the **start** of implementing or updating any web UI, CSS layout/animation, or client-side JS logic (dates/timezones, sanitization, performance, accessibility, UX fixes) before writing ad-hoc solutions or adding dependencies.

## Primary Workflow

### Step 1. Search Use Cases

Run `modern-web-guidance` directly with `npx` using a **2–5 word action-oriented query** for a **single web platform capability or UI pattern**:
- **Keep queries focused and generic**: Describe the user-visible capability (`<verb> + <UI/platform object>`, optionally paired with the target HTML/CSS/JS feature name if known). Omit framework/library names (`React`, `Vue`, `Tailwind`, etc.) and app/domain nouns (product, route, or component/file names). Split multi-feature tasks into separate `search` calls.
- **Name implied UI primitives**: When the user's prompt expresses intent without naming the UI primitive (e.g. "confirm first", "delete with confirmation", "pick a date"), translate the domain intent into the implied UI component or platform mechanism (e.g. search `"confirmation modal dialog"` or `"confirm dialog"` rather than `"confirm destructive action"`, or `"date picker input"` rather than `"pick a date"`).
- **Example**: Search `"light dismiss dialog"` or `"responsive data table"`, **not** `"dialog"` (too terse), `"responsive table dark mode"` (compound — split into two searches), or `"close React settings modal on outside click"` (framework/app noise).

```sh
npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest search "<query>" --skill-version 2026_11_09-5bcc021b
```

> **Note**: Returns `[{ "id", "description" }, ...]`. Judge results by their `description` fields:
> - **Match found**: Call `retrieve` directly—do not also run `list`.
> - **Weak or empty results**: If `search` returns `[]` or unrelated descriptions, **rephrase `search` once** using the concrete HTML/CSS/UI component noun or synonym (e.g., `dialog`, `modal`, `popover`, `table`, `form`) before falling back to `list` (or use `list` once for broad UI audits).
> - **Topic not covered**: If no `description` matches after rephrasing, proceed without retrieving unrelated guides.

### Step 2. Retrieve Best Practices

Once you have relevant `id`(s) from the search results, call `retrieve` to get the full guide(s)—including both specific use-case guides that match your task and any broader discipline guide (e.g., `html`, `css`, `forms`, `accessibility`, `color`, `performance`, `security`) that applies. You can pass multiple IDs separated by commas.

```sh
npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "<id>"
```

If `retrieve` saves large output (> 9.5 KB) to a temporary file to prevent truncation, read that file path in full using your file-reading tool (reading remaining line ranges if needed)—do not use `cat` or `head`.

### Step 3. Verify Guidance Compliance

When generating or modifying code, cross-check the implementation against the retrieved guide before concluding:
- **Applicable Guidance & Fallbacks**: Ensure the relevant modern patterns and necessary fallback strategies from the guide are correctly applied, without forcing unrequested features.
- **Task Fulfillment**: Confirm that the implementation fully satisfies the user's request.
- Do not run `legacy-scan`; it's for detecting legacy patterns to modernize, not this.

### Step 4. Disclose Skill Usage

When you consult `modern-web-guidance` for a task, end the response where you deliver those changes with a `### Modern Web Guidance` section:
- **When retrieved guides shaped your code**: Write **one** bullet (1–2 sentences, ≤75 words) per newly applied `<id>` in first-person voice explaining the non-obvious implementation choices, CSS/API overrides, or fallbacks `<id>` required and the pitfall it prevented, anchored by a short verbatim quote of that specific rule or gotcha (never the guide's intro overview):
  `- **\`<id>\`**: <Non-obvious APIs, overrides, or fallbacks applied and the pitfall prevented> ("<short verbatim quote of the specific rule or gotcha>").`
  - **Never** guess `<id>`s or quotes from memory after context compaction (re-run `search`/`retrieve` if needed), and credit **only** guide-backed changes from the current turn.
- **When searched/listed in this turn but zero guides applied**: Write one first-person sentence naming which topics or guides you checked in `modern-web-guidance` and why none applied (omit if any guide applied).

## Alternative flow: Modernize an existing codebase

**Only** when asked for a broad, open-ended codebase modernization or legacy-pattern scan where no specific target feature or component is named (do **not** run `legacy-scan` when asked to add, update, fix, or audit a specific feature or component), run the 4-step modernization flow:

> **Note**: `legacy-scan` scans for a curated subset (~20% of the guidance corpus).

```sh
npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan <path> --json
```

1. Scan: Run `legacy-scan <path> --json` to detect legacy web platform patterns across the project or directory.
2. Verify: Check each finding against its `keepWhen` / `dropWhen` rubric; drop false positives (fallbacks, cross-file helpers, vendor code, lookalikes).
3. Report: Summarize verified findings (and the modernization plan, if editing) for the user, noting that `legacy-scan` only checks the subset of guides (~20% of the catalog) that have deterministic legacy rules.
4. Modernize (when the user asked to modernize rather than only audit/report): Retrieve each finding's guide (`retrieve "<guide-id>"` via Step 2), apply the replacement (keeping existing libraries as fallbacks where the guide requires one), and re-run `legacy-scan <path>` on the modified files to confirm resolution.
   - Dropped findings and kept fallbacks still match static scans; do not edit safe code or inspect `legacy-scan.mjs` to force 0 findings.

## Using npx / pnpx

- **Runner & Permissions**: Prefer `pnpx` over `npx` if `pnpm` is available (`pnpx` does not use `-y`); on Windows, use `npx.cmd`. When requesting tool permissions, allowlist `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest *` (or `pnpx modern-web-guidance@latest *`) specifically, never bare `npx *` or `pnpx *`.
- **Sandboxes & Network**: Fetching `modern-web-guidance` requires outbound network access. In sandboxed or approval-gated environments (e.g., Codex, Claude Code), **proactively request approval/allowlisting with network access BEFORE the first execution** to avoid timeouts, and set `NPM_CONFIG_CACHE=/tmp/npm-cache` if `~/.npm` is read-only.
- **Offline**: If the command hangs due to being offline, retry with `npx --offline …`.

## Guidelines

- Always search **first** to find the most relevant guides. Do not hallucinate guides or ignore them; they represent the preferred local standard for the user's project.
- These guides use vanilla HTML/CSS/JS; adapt them to your framework without dropping the modern feature:
  - **Types**: Spread/cast newly shipped HTML attributes (`{...({ popover: 'hint', interestfor: id, commandfor: id, switch: '' } as any)}`, `[attr.*]`) rather than removing them or merging `@types/react`.
  - **SSR & Bundlers**: Guard `window`/`HTMLElement` in SSR and load polyfills via bare `import('<pkg>')` in client effects (or set Vite `build.target: 'esnext'` for top-level `await`)—never copy files from `node_modules`.
  - **DOM, IDs & CSS**: Call `showModal()`/`moveBefore()` via refs on non-VDOM-managed nodes, generate per-instance IDs/`anchor-name`s (`useId()`), and keep `:root` and `@starting-style` top-level/unscoped.

## Interpreting Browser Support & Fallbacks

* **Default Behavior**: All guides assume **Baseline Widely available** features are safe to use without fallbacks. For features that are not Baseline widely available, you **MUST** follow the fallback recommendations in the guide, unless the user has specified a custom browser support policy.
* **Custom Policies**: If the user defines explicit browser support requirements, use the guide's compatibility data to determine if a fallback can be ignored (for `Baseline YYYY` targets, a feature satisfies the target if its "Baseline since" date is `<= YYYY`). Examples: _"Do not implement feature fallbacks"_, _"Safari 17.4+"_, _"Never implement polyfills; use a lightweight custom fallback or redesign"_, or _"Allow Newly Available features if feature-detected with graceful degradation"_.
* **Reactive Policy Discovery**: Suggest documenting a policy in `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` (e.g., `**Browser Support:** Allow Newly Available features, but only adopt custom fallback code that adds <= 20 lines and no external dependencies`) if the developer targets a restricted runtime (Electron/Tauri), excludes specific browsers, hesitates over polyfill size/complexity, or asks if a feature is safe without fallbacks.

Content Navigability and Structure ### Landmarks - **Place all content within landmarks:** Wrap each relevant part of the page in `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<aside>`, and `<footer>` elements so assistive-tech users can jump between regions. (1.3.6 Identify Purpose (Level AAA)) - **Use the correct landmark:** Use the `<header>` element as a container for introductory content, the `<nav>` element as a container for site-wide or in-page navigation links, the `<main>` element as a container for the main content of the page, the `<aside>` element as a container for content that is tangentially related to the main content, and the `<footer>` element as a container for information about the related content, such as the author, copyright information, and links to related documents. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Use one `<main>` landmark per page:** Avoid using multiple `<main>` elements on a single page. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Provide distinguishable accessible names for navigation regions:** If a page contains multiple `<nav>` elements, apply the `aria-label` attribute to each element and set its value to a distinguishable accessible name for the region. For example: `<nav aria-label="Primary">`, `<nav aria-label="Secondary">`, and so on. (Best practice) - **Don't overuse landmarks:** Too many landmarks dilute their value. In particular, avoid labeling a `<section>` (which turns it into a `region` landmark) — `region` should be a last resort when no other landmark fits. (Best practice) ### Headings - **Structure main content with headings:** Use `<h1>`–`<h6>` elements sequentially so screen reader users get a navigable outline. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Mandatory - Don't use "fake" headings:** Never use `<div>` or `<span>` elements to look like headings without standard `<h1>`–`<h6>` elements. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Avoid nesting headings incorrectly:** Make sure that, if a sub-heading is visually less important than its parent heading, its heading level is lower in the heading hierarchy. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Use one `<h1>` element per page:** Use the `<h1>` element for the page's main heading. Having more than one `<h1>` element on a page makes it difficult for screen reader users to identify the actual main heading. (Best Practice) - **Caveat:** If a page includes a modal dialog that is marked up using the `<dialog>` element, `role="dialog"`, or `role="alertdialog"`, it is fine to mark up its main heading using the `<h1>` element because the dialog is a new window that is separate from the page. - **Avoid "skipped" heading levels:** Avoid jumping directly from (for example) `<h1>` → `<h4>` to avoid breaking the logical hierarchy. (Best Practice) - **Avoid placing headings inside the `<summary>` element:** Some browsers still expose this element as a button, which removes all roles from its children including headings. If a heading must act as a disclosure trigger, use an accordion or a disclosure implemented with ARIA where the heading element wraps the button, rather than use the `<details>` and `<summary>` elements. (Best Practice) ### Lists - **Use lists for repeated, contiguous content:** `<ul>`/`<ol>` give assistive tech a count of listitems up front and let users skip the entire list. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Use the correct list element:** Use the `<ul>` element for unordered lists where the order of the items is **not** important (such as a list of related products), and use the `<ol>` element for ordered lists where the order of the content **is** important (such as a list of instructions). (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Don't use lists for non-list content:** Do not use list markup to mark up separate paragraphs of text, as screen readers will announce list information when they encounter lists, therefore leading to a screen reader hearing potentially confusing and redundant information about the related content. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Don't use lists for checkboxes and radio buttons:** When marked up correctly, screen readers will already announce the number of checkboxes or radio buttons, as well as the number of the currently focused checkbox / radio button in the set, even though there is no list markup. Additional list markup will lead to duplication. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) ### Tables - **Do use the correct table elements:** Use the `<table>` element to identify the table, the `<caption>` element to provide a title and accessible name for the description, the `<tr>` element to identify individual rows in the table, and the `<th>` and `<td>` elements to identify header and data cells respectively. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Do use the `scope` attribute on `<th>` elements:** The `scope` attribute indicates whether the `<th>` element represents a row header (`<th scope="row">`) or a column header (`<th scope="col">`). (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Mandatory - Don't use tables for layout:** Screen readers will announce redundant information about the layout, which may be confusing for screen reader users, while the use of tabular markup has an impact on the reading and keyboard focus order of content. Use CSS Grid/Flexbox for visual layouts instead. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Avoid overly-complex tables:** Spanned rows, spanned columns, nested tables, and expandable / collapsible rows can make sense visually and meet the related WCAG success criterion, but the overall structure can be disorienting and difficult to navigate for screen reader users. In such cases, break tables up into smaller tables that are easier and more efficient to navigate. (Best Practice) ### Skip links - **Provide skip links** prior to repeated content like site headers with navigation or long/infinite lists, so that keyboard users can easily bypass them. (2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (Level A)) - **Caveat:** Sometimes screen magnifiers do not follow the focus when a skip link’s target is not normally focusable. The recommended workaround is to make the target programmatically focusable, but not a part of the tab order, using `tabindex="-1"`. If the target contains focusable elements, this creates another usability issue as clicking within the target will always set the **sequential focus navigation start point** to the target rather than at a point between focusable elements. A solution that satisfies both user expectations is to make the first meaningful element within the intended target the actual target of the skip link with `tabindex="-1"`, for example a heading (`<h1 id="content" tabindex="-1">`). Beware that any content prior to such an element will be skipped, including other relevant content within the targeted section, and this creates usability gaps for other assistive tech users. - **Avoid using skip links where they are not needed:** A set of pages whose only common element is a single link to the Home page does not need a skip link. (Best Practice) - **Avoid overusing skip links:** A single skip link, or two skip links to cover the primary and secondary sets of common navigation links, is usually sufficient on a single page. Multiple unnecessary skip links add to the number of <kbd>Tab</kbd> stops to a page, which causes frustration for people who use the keyboard alone for navigation. (Best Practice) ```html <!-- Good: Skip to main content --> <a href="#content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a> <main id="content">...</main> ``` ### Code Example: good use of landmarks, headings, lists, tables, and a skip link ```html <!-- Good: Semantic landmarks, heading hierarchy, skip link --> <header> <a href="#platform-dashboard" class="skip-link visually-hidden">Skip to content</a> <nav aria-label="Primary"> <ul> <li><a href="/">Home</a></li> </ul> </nav> </header> <main> <h1 id="platform-dashboard" tabindex="-1">Platform Dashboard</h1> <section> <h2>User Statistics</h2> <table> <caption>Monthly active users</caption> <thead> <tr> <th scope="col">Month</th> <th scope="col">Users</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>January</td> <td>12,000</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h3>Notes</h3> <ul> <li>Results do not include users without active subscriptions</li> <li>Results are accurate as of 31 December 2025</li> </ul> </section> </main> ``` ## 2. Semantic HTML and ARIA ### Prefer native HTML - **Prefer HTML elements and attributes to ARIA:** Avoid `<div role="button">` or `<a role="button">` and use `<button>` instead. Native HTML elements and attributes already have the correct role and behavior, including keyboard support, built-in by default. `<button>` already implies `role="button"`, `required` already implies `aria-required`, and no additional JavaScript is required to ensure the correct role and behavior is supported. (Best Practice) - **Caveat:** ARIA is required when the related feature is not available in HTML, for example there are no HTML elements explicitly intended for building a tabbed navigation widget, but ARIA includes appropriate role and state properties for this purpose. - **Don't add redundant ARIA roles or properties:** Avoid `<ul role="list">`, `<nav role="navigation">`, and `<input required aria-required="true">`. (Best Practice) - **Caveat:** Safari removes list semantics from `<ul>`/`<ol>` outside `<nav>` when `list-style: none` or `display: flex`/`grid` is applied. In that case `role="list"` is required to restore them. - **Don't apply interactive ARIA roles to structural HTML elements:** Use `<li><span role="button">Button in a list</span></li>`, not `<li role="button">Button in a list</li>`, to avoid breaking the container list semantics. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Caveat:** It is acceptable to apply ARIA roles to structural HTML elements that have similar semantics, for example a tree view: `<ul role="tree"><li role="treeitem">…</li>…</ul>`. ### ARIA roles and states - **Match ARIA implementations to actual behavior:** When applying `role="tab"` to an element, it must then behave like a tab — including keyboard interactions. Many ARIA patterns can't be implemented in CSS alone and need JavaScript. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Manage toggle states:** Utilize `aria-expanded` and `aria-pressed` to communicate toggle states for custom controls. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Be deliberate about `disabled` vs `aria-disabled`:** `disabled` removes the element from the focus order entirely (and `tabindex="0"` won't bring it back), which is often wrong for toolbar buttons or links. `aria-disabled="true"` keeps the element focusable so users can land on it and learn it's disabled, but because it only communicates state to assistive technologies, you must also prevent activation (such as pointer clicks and keyboard triggers) in JavaScript. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Mandatory - Don't hide interactive elements from screen readers:** Do not apply `aria-hidden="true"` to interactive elements that receive focus, or to their parent elements. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Mandatory - Don't suppress the roles of interactive elements:** Applying `role="presentation"` or `role="none"` to an interactive element strips its semantics. The element will still be exposed to assistive technologies and announced by screen readers, but its role and any state information will not be, which results in confusion and potentially unexpected behavior. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Don't assume custom elements have no ARIA:** Custom elements can attach ARIA via `ElementInternals`, which some automated test tools can't see — so the absence of `role`/`aria-*` attributes in markup doesn't prove the element has no semantics. Verify with the browser's accessibility-tree inspector. (Best Practice) ## 3. Accessible Names and Descriptions Every interactive element and some landmarks need an accessible name, and many benefit from an accessible description. Names are short and identify the element; descriptions add context. ### Naming mechanisms - **Prefer native naming mechanisms:** `<label>` for form controls, `<caption>` for `<table>`, `<legend>` for `<fieldset>`, `<figcaption>` for `<figure>`. (Best Practice) - **Explicitly associate `<label>` with its control via `for`/`id`:** As well as ensuring the control is appropriately labeled by the contents of the `<label>` element, this results in a larger target area for people to activate the label _or_ its related control to move focus to the control, which isn't globally supported with other forms of labeling (such as using the `aria-labelledby` attribute). Additionally, some assistive technologies, particularly voice recognition software, require the `for`/`id` relationship to be explicitly set, even if an equivalent accessibility-supported approach (such as nesting an `<input>` inside a `<label>`) is taken. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Prefer `aria-labelledby` over `aria-label` when a visible label exists:** This avoids duplication, improves maintainability, and translates better. (Best Practice) - **Don't use `title` as a naming mechanism:** The value of this attribute is only displayed on mouse hover, and cannot be displayed or otherwise accessed using the keyboard in any browser. (Best Practice) - **Caveat:** `<iframe>` is an exception, as the `title` attribute is the standard way of providing an accessible name for this element. - **Don't use `placeholder` as a naming mechanism:** While the value of this attribute is initially displayed inside an `<input>` or `<textarea>`, it disappears as soon as the user enters text into the field, meaning that there is no longer a visual cue as to what the field represents. The contrast between `placeholder` text and its background in most browsers is very low, and therefore is difficult for people to perceive. (3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A)) - **Don't put `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` on elements that shouldn't be named:** Examples include plain `<div>`, `<span>`, and other custom elements without a role. These attributes are only intended for providing accessible names for elements that have explicit or implicit widget (for example, button, link, and tab), landmark, image, or iframe roles. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Caveat:** Custom elements may have an implicit role set via `ElementInternals`, so the absence of a `role` attribute isn't conclusive. ### Choosing the name - **Avoid inconsistent link text:** If multiple hyperlinks direct users to the same target page, make sure each link has the same accessible name, which should typically be the same as its visible link text. For example, if the target page for a link is `profile.html`, make sure that all links have an accessible name of "My Profile" **or** "Profile"; do not use "My Profile" in one instance, and "Profile" in the other. (Best Practice) - **Disambiguate controls that look visually identical but which perform different actions by their accessible name:** For example, a page may include multiple "Edit" buttons, each of which triggers functionality to perform a different action, such as edit the user's name, edit the user's password, and edit the user's address. While it may be visually obvious from the surrounding content what the purpose of these buttons might be, screen reader users may only hear "Edit, button". Techniques to resolve this include the following: (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Use visually hidden text:** The text is included in the DOM but is visually hidden using CSS. For example `<button>Edit <span class="visually-hidden">first name</span></button>`. Refer to the [code example: visually hidden utility](#code-example-visually-hidden-utility) for the full CSS. - **Apply the `aria-label` attribute to the control:** The value of this attribute should then include the visible text as well as important contextual information, for example `<button aria-label="Edit name">Edit</button>`, `<button aria-label="Edit address">Edit</button>`, and so on. - **Use the `aria-labelledby` or `aria-describedby` attribute to associate the control with the content it relates to:** Chaining IDs in `aria-labelledby` appends the related text to the control's accessible name (for example, `<p id="firstName">First name</p> <button id="editFirstName" aria-labelledby="editFirstName firstName">Edit</button>`), whereas `aria-describedby` provides the context as an accessible description (`<p id="firstName">First name</p> <button aria-describedby="firstName">Edit</button>`). - **Do include a control's visible text in its accessible name:** Any visible text used to label a control must be included exactly as written in the control's accessible name. The accessible name can include additional information before or after the visible text, but the visible text itself must not differ. For example, the accessible name for a link containing the link phrase "Read more" can be "Read more about [subject]", because the visible text is included without modification. However, the accessible name cannot be "Read some more about [subject]", because the term "some" appears between the words "Read" and "more", which is not reflected in the visible text. (2.5.3 Label in Name (Level A)) - **Don't reuse an accessible name across controls with different effects in the same view:** Make sure that each accessible name is disambiguated. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Caveat:** Having two separate buttons with the accessible name of "Close" in two separate dialog boxes is fine, because only one dialog box is reachable at a time; however, multiple "Edit" buttons for different effects in the same dialog box is not. - **Don't reuse an accessible name across hyperlinks that point to different `href` targets:** For example, avoid `<a href="annualreport2025.html">Annual Report</a>` and `<a href="annualreport2026.html">Annual Report</a>`. Use `<a href="annualreport2025.html">Annual Report 2025</a>` and `<a href="annualreport2026.html">Annual Report 2026</a>` (or an equivalent technique for disambiguating controls) instead. - **Don't pack descriptions, error messages, or instructions into the label:** Verbose labels confuse and frustrate people who use screen readers. Instead, use the `aria-describedby` attribute to programmatically associate any additional content with the field. For example: `<label for="yourComments">Your comments</label><p id="yourCommentsWarning">Please do not include any personal information in this field.</p><textarea id="yourComments" aria-describedby="yourCommentsWarning"></textarea>`. Screen readers will then announce the label first, followed by the control type, and only then announce additional information that a user can skip if they are already aware of it. (Best Practice) - **Don't repeat state information already exposed by ARIA inside the label:** Examples include information exposed via the `aria-expanded`, `aria-checked`, `aria-selected`, `aria-pressed`, and similar attributes. This creates duplication, redundancy, and ambiguity. (Best Practice) - **Don't include the role name in the label:** This will lead to duplication. For example, `<nav aria-label="Primary navigation">` will be read by screen readers as "Primary navigation, navigation". (Best Practice) ### Descriptions - **Identify instructions, error messages, and any other important information explicitly related to a control as a description:** Examples of descriptions include: (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - A list of password requirements when creating an account - An error message related to a field in a previously submitted form - Additional instructions, such as "You must agree to the terms and conditions before you can submit the form" - **Make sure the description is available to assistive technologies when the related element receives focus:** Take one of the following approaches (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)): - If the description is already visible on the page, programmatically associate it with the element using the `aria-describedby` attribute. - If the description is not visible on the page and is explicitly for screen reader users (in other words, when providing a visible description is not appropriate or useful), apply the `aria-description` attribute to the element and use it to provide an appropriate description. - **Avoid including a description for every element:** if the primary label already provides sufficient information (such as "First name"), any additional description is likely to be redundant. (Best Practice) - **Caveat:** Inline error messages associated with controls, such as error messages below / above text fields, as well as secondary labels that should be announced when the element receives focus, are exceptions. - **Avoid including information in the description that is already provided by attributes applied to the element:** For example, including "This is a required field" as a description for an `<input>` element that already includes the `required` attribute will lead to duplicate announcements. (Best Practice) - **Caveat:** `aria-invalid="true"` is an exception; many screen readers announce "invalid" when they reach an `<input>` that includes this attribute set to `true`, which indicates that the field is in error. However, it does not indicate what the error is. In such cases, a description (the actual human readable error message) is required. This attribute should only be applied and set to true when the error message is present. - **Avoid including interactive elements in an `aria-describedby` target** unless the content of the element reads sensibly as a description on its own. For example: (Best Practice) - This is acceptable, as the entire text string makes sense when announced: `<p id="description">I understand the <a href="tandc.html">terms and conditions</a>.</p>` - This is not appropriate, as the description will be announced as "Please don't include personal information in this field. Learn more.", where "Learn more" will be announced out of its intended context: `<p id="description">Please don't include personal information in this field. <a href="…">Learn more</a></p>`. Instead, only include the plain text in the referenced description: `<p><span id="description">Please don't include personal information in this field.</span> <a href="…">Learn more</a></p>`. ### Code Example: Visually Hidden Utility A `.visually-hidden` utility provides text for screen readers without rendering it visually. It's commonly used for skip links, additional context on icon-only buttons, and supplementary labels. ```css /* Hides content visually but keeps it in the accessibility tree. :focus-within / :active opt elements out — useful for skip links and any focusable content wrapped in this class. */ .visually-hidden:where(:not(:focus-within, :active)) { position: absolute !important; clip-path: inset(50%) !important; overflow: hidden !important; width: 1px !important; height: 1px !important; margin: -1px !important; padding: 0 !important; border: 0 !important; white-space: nowrap !important; } ``` When the hidden content is focusable (skip links, focus-receiving wrappers), the `:focus-within`/`:active` exception lets it become visible. Style the visible state per situation, e.g. a skip link to the main content typically wants fixed positioning at the top-left of the viewport so the rest of the page doesn't shift. ## 4. Document Metadata and Language ### Language - **Do declare the page's human language:** Always apply the `lang` attribute to the page's `<html>` element, and always set it to the primary human language of the page's content. For example, `<html lang="en">`. (3.1.1 Language of Page (Level A)) - **Do declare changes in the page's human language:** If there is a language change on the page, apply the `lang` attribute to the parent/container element for the affected content, and set the value of this attribute to the shortcode for the language of the affected content. For example: `<p>In Germany, you may be greeted by someone saying <span lang="de">Guten Morgen</span>.</p>`. (3.1.2 Language of Parts (Level AA)) - **Don't set the value of the `lang` attribute to a value that doesn't match the human language of the content:** This causes screen readers and other text-to-speech software to announce the content in a non-understandable manner. (3.1.1 Language of Page (Level A), 3.1.2 Language of Parts (Level AA)) ### Titles - **Do include the `<title>` element in the `<head>` section for all pages:** This includes pages embedded into a document using an `<iframe>`. (2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A)) - **Provide unique page titles:** Every page should have its own title that unambiguously reflects the page's purpose or content. (2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A)) - **Front-load the page's `<title>` with unique content:** For example, `<title>Page Topic | Site Name`. (Best Practice) - **Update single-page application (SPA) titles during page transitions:** For example, if the page title is `Contact Us` when a contact form is displayed, update the title to `Thank you for contacting us!` when the form is successfully submitted. (2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A)) - **Don't include an empty `` element in the `<head>` section of a page:** No matter how short or inconsequential a page appears, do not use `<title>`. Page titles appear in the browser tab, so pages are distinguishable when users have multiple tabs open, and are typically announced by screen readers when the page is opened. (2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A)) - **Avoid using the same title for multiple pages, or using ambiguous page titles:** In such cases, pages are indistinguishable without reviewing the actual page content itself. (2.4.2 Page Titled (Level A)) ### Iframes - **Do provide a descriptive `title` for ` ``` ## 5. Keyboard and Focus Management ### Tab order and focusability - **Provide a logical tab order:** Make sure that the order in which elements receive focus follows an appropriate sequence. (2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A)) - **Caveat:** In left-to-right reading languages, the tab order is logical when focus moves from top-to-bottom and left-to-right. However, in right-to-left reading languages, the tab order is logical when focus moves from top-to-bottom and right-to-left. - **Use `tabindex` only when necessary:** Apply `tabindex="0"` to elements requiring focus where an appropriate interactive role has been applied but the element isn't focusable by default; for example, `Print` (2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A)) - **Manage focus correctly to and from updated content:** For example, if a dialog box appears on the page, make sure that focus immediately moves to the dialog box, is restricted to the contents of the dialog box, and (when dismissed) returns to the element that originally triggered the dialog box. # Accessible generated content

- **DON'T** use `content` to convey meaningful text (labels, state, instructions) — keep that in the DOM (WCAG F87). The alt text argument is harm reduction for cases where decoration accidentally carries meaning, not a license.
- Use the alternative text argument of `content` to provide alt text for screen readers. E.g. `content: url(cloud.svg) / "Save";`
- Use `content: "text" / "";` to prevent purely decorative text from being announced to screen readers.
- **DON'T** use an empty alt text argument for images — they're already presentational by default. E.g. this is wrong: `content: url(cloud.svg) / "";`.
- **DON'T** use the alt text argument to describe emojis unless the description differs from the official emoji name. E.g. don't do `content: "🎉" / "celebration";`, but `content: "🎉" / "Yay!";` is fine.

**ONLY** use the alt text argument when the text is different than the primary value and is not already present in the DOM. I.e. this is wrong:

HTML:
```html
<button class="save">Save</button>
```

CSS:
```css
button.save::before {
  content: url(cloud.svg) / "Save";
}
```

A screen reader would read it out as "Save save".

## Fallback strategies

Baseline status for Alt text for generated content: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2024-07-09.
Supported by: Chrome 77 (Sep 2019), Edge 79 (Jan 2020), Firefox 128 (Jul 2024), and Safari 17.4 (Mar 2024).

If your Baseline target includes browsers that do not support the `/` alternative text syntax, precede the declaration with a single-value `content` fallback so unsupported browsers do not drop the entire declaration as invalid CSS:

```css
.more-link::after {
  /* Fallback: render the glyph in browsers without `/` support
     (screen readers there will still announce it) */
  content: " →";
  content: " →" / "";
}
```

For non-empty alternative text (`content: url(...) / "..."`), a single-value `content: url(...)` fallback keeps the image visible in older browsers but drops its alt text. If that label is required in older browsers, put it in the DOM instead (e.g., via a visually hidden `<span>` or `aria-label`) and use a plain `content: url(...)` declaration without `/`.

[8 Grid lanes (aka masonry)](#8-grid-lanes-aka-masonry) ## 1 Fundamentals Lean on the browser's layout engine when possible for better performance. Reach for intrinsic sizing, logical properties, and `aspect-ratio` before resorting to hardcoded dimensions or complicated media-queries. ### 1.1 Which layout mode to use? Walk the decision tree top-to-bottom and stop at the first match. Note that layouts can be nested within each-other and each decision is based on the use-case for that container. 1. **Is it a simple row OR column of items?** Use **flexbox** — 1D, content-first, content distributes along a single axis. 2. **Does a nested element need to line up with its grandparent grid's tracks?** Use **subgrid** — 2D, relationship-first, inherits parent tracks so grandchildren can align across siblings. 3. **Is it a complex page or component structure with rows AND columns?** Use **grid** — 2D, layout-first, you define the skeleton and content fills it. 4. **Is the content a long flow of prose that should split into balanced columns?** Use **multi-column** — 1D flow, newspaper-style. 5. **Are items of varied heights that need to be packed tightly?** Use **grid** with `grid-auto-flow: dense` today; reach for native masonry (aka "grid lanes") only when it ships in your Baseline target (see [§8](#8-grid-lanes-aka-masonry)). 6. **Does an element need to float above the page and stay spatially tethered to a trigger, even across DOM boundaries or stacking contexts?** Use **anchor positioning** — `anchor-name` on the trigger, `position-anchor` on the overlay (see [§5](#5-native-overlays-anchor-positioning-and-stacking-contexts)). ### 1.2 Working principles - Use logical properties (`inline-size`, `block-size`, `margin-inline`, `padding-block`, `inset-inline-start`) for layout dimensions and spacing — see `css` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "css"`) for full coverage. - Apply the content-first vs layout-first mental model: flexbox when items dictate flow, grid when you define the skeleton first. - Use the `place-*` shorthands (`place-content`, `place-items`, `place-self`) to align across both axes in one declaration. - Reach for intrinsic sizing (`min-content`, `max-content`, `fit-content()`) and flexible tracks (`fr`, `minmax()`) before fixed `width`/`height` — fewer media queries, more resilient layouts. - Do NOT use `overflow: hidden` to mask layout issues — fix them at the source. For example certain replaced elements like ``, ``, `

`. ```css /* Align grid-template-areas in rows and columns for readability. */ .page-layout { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); grid-template-areas: "header header header" "sidebar main main" "footer footer footer"; gap: 1.5rem; } header { grid-area: header; } aside { grid-area: sidebar; } footer { grid-area: footer; } .card-grid { grid-area: main; display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(240px, 1fr)); grid-template-rows: auto 1fr; /* title block, body block */ gap: 1rem; } .card { grid-row: span 2; display: grid; /* Same-cascade fallback: ignored when subgrid is supported. */ grid-template-rows: auto 1fr; grid-template-rows: subgrid; } ``` ## 4 Container queries Baseline status for Container queries (size): Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2023-02-14. Supported by: Chrome 105 (Sep 2022), Edge 105 (Sep 2022), Firefox 110 (Feb 2023), and Safari 16 (Sep 2022). Query the size (or computed style) of an ancestor container rather than the viewport. Mental model: container queries = component context; media queries = global page layout and user preferences (`prefers-color-scheme`, `prefers-reduced-motion`). **Do:** - Establish a containment context with `container-type: inline-size` (width-only queries) or `container-type: size` (both axes) on a wrapper before its descendants can be queried. - Name containers with `container-name` (or the `container` shorthand: `container: card / inline-size`) when nested contexts could collide. - Include container query units in calculating fluid type and spacing: `cqi`/`cqb` (logical inline/block), `cqw`/`cqh` (physical), `cqmin`/`cqmax`. - Give the container a definite `block-size` whenever `container-type: size` is used — without one, descendants collapse because size containment forces the container to ignore its content. **Do not:** - Don't use `block-size` as a `container-type` value — it isn't valid. Use `size` for both axes. - Don't expect children's intrinsic size to influence the container after declaring `container-type`. The container is computed as if it has no children once containment is active. - Don't rely on container query units inside descendants of a non-qualifying ancestor; they fall back to the small viewport (`svw`/`svh`). ### 4.1 Code example: fluid typography using container query units ```css .card-wrapper { container: card / inline-size; /* shorthand for container-name / container-type */ } @container card (inline-size > 400px) { .content { display: flex; gap: 2rem; } } .title { /* Fluid type bound to the container width, not the viewport. */ font-size: clamp(1rem, 4cqi, 2rem); } ``` > For component-driven responsive styling patterns, see `size-aware-styling` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "size-aware-styling"`) and `fluid-scaling` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "fluid-scaling"`). ## 5 Native overlays, anchor positioning, and stacking contexts Baseline status for : Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2022-03-14. Supported by: Chrome 37 (Aug 2014), Edge 79 (Jan 2020), Firefox 98 (Mar 2022), and Safari 15.4 (Mar 2022). Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27. Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS 18.3 (Jan 2025). Browser support for Anchor positioning: Limited availability. Supported by: Safari 27 (Sep 2026). Unsupported in: Chrome, Edge, and Firefox. **When to use each overlay primitive:** - Use `popover` for transient, non-modal UI (flyouts, toasts, tooltips) — lives in the top layer, no `z-index` management needed. - Use `` with `.showModal()` for modal interactions that require focus trapping and an inert backdrop. - Don't combine `popover` and `.showModal()` on the same element — they're mutually exclusive runtime states. **Anchor positioning (spatial layout of overlays):** - Use `position-area` (or `anchor()` on insets) and `anchor-size()` to position and size an overlay relative to its trigger. - Use `position-try-fallbacks: flip-block` (or `flip-inline`) to let the browser reposition when the overlay overflows the viewport. - Don't mix physical and logical keywords in a single `position-area` value — pick one coordinate system. - Feature-detect with `@supports (anchor-name: --x)` and provide an absolute-position fallback. > For full implementation detail, polyfill strategies, and `popover` value reference, see `declarative-dialog-popover-control` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "declarative-dialog-popover-control"`) and `position-aware-tooltips` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "position-aware-tooltips"`). For anchor positioning applied to dropdowns, flyouts, and tab indicators, see `viewport-aware-dropdowns` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "viewport-aware-dropdowns"`) and `anchor-positioning-tab-underline` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "anchor-positioning-tab-underline"`). ## 6 Overflow tracking and layout stability Baseline status for scrollbar-gutter: Newly available. ## 1. Foundations

Be allergic to knowledge duplication. Prefer variables over repetition, but whenever possible, prefer built-in conventions such as:
- `currentColor` instead of defining a variable and setting `color` to it
- The `inherit` keyword instead of defining a variable on the parent and using it on the same property across parent and child.
- `em` units instead of `font-size: var(--size)`
- `cqw`/`cqh` (or their logical versions — `cqi`/`cqb`) units instead of repeating box model values.
- Code duplication is not knowledge duplication. The goal is robustness and maintainability, not saving characters.
- Prefer **logical properties and values** over physical ones (e.g. `margin-inline-start` instead of `margin-left`) so that styles adapt to different writing modes and orientations. Even if the page author does not plan to localize, external translation tools often display translated text in context.
- Do not use logical properties indiscriminately — ask yourself "would I want this to flip in RTL?" — if the answer is no, use the physical property instead.
- Consider different viewing modes (dark mode, high contrast mode), different viewport sizes, and different input modes (touch, keyboard, pointer).

## 2. Inheritance and The Cascade

**Avoid** introducing BEM naming conventions to manage specificity.
Instead, use modern CSS features such as cascade layers and `:where()` to make cascade behavior predictable and follow author intent.

Use cascade layers (`@layer`) to define explicit priority zones (e.g., `reset`, `base`, `theme`, `components`, `utilities`), and declare their order upfront (e.g. `@layer reset, base, theme, components, utilities;`).
Within each layer, use `:where()` to make selectors only compete based on meaningful signals, not incidental filters (`:not()` edge cases, remote ancestors, etc.) or for one-off easily overridable defaults.

Use keywords like `inherit`, `initial`, `unset`, or `revert` instead of explicit values to improve maintainability and better express intent.
Examples:
- When specifying a transition on a child that should match the parent's `transition-*` properties, instead of repeating the transition properties on the child, use `transition: inherit` (reduce duplication, improve maintainability)
- Use `initial` to reset a property to its initial value instead of specifying the value explicitly (clearer expression of intent)

## 3. Selectors and scoping

Modern browser-native selectors reduce the need for preprocessors and complex state-tracking in JS.

### Prefer CSS selectors over JS for complex element targeting

- **DO** use `:has()` to style parents based on child state instead of managing classes in JS (e.g. `label:has(:checked)` instead of a manual `label.has-checked` class) For more information, see the guides at `child-state-based-styling` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "child-state-based-styling"`) and `content-based-styling` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "content-based-styling"`).
- **DO NOT** nest `:has()` or use pseudo-elements inside it (browser API limitation)
- Use `:nth-child(<An+B> of <selector>)` when you need to style every n-th element of a certain type. E.g. `details:nth-child(1 of [open])` will style the first open `<details>` element it finds, whereas `details[open]:first-child` would style only the first child if and only if it was open.

### Use `:is()` (or `:where()`) instead of CSS rule duplication for fallbacks

**DO NOT** duplicate CSS rules to provide fallbacks for pseudo-classes that may not be supported — use `:is()` or `:where()` instead and take advantage of their forgiving parsing rules.

```css
/* BAD: duplicate rules instead of using `:where()` */
[popover]:popover-open {
  /* styles for native popovers */
}
[popover].\:popover-open {
  /* same styles again, for polyfilled popovers */
}

/* GOOD */
[popover]:where(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) {
  /* same styles in one rule */
}
```

Do NOT use this for pseudo-elements, as they are not supported in `:is()` or `:where()`.

### Avoid overmatching

Write selectors in a way that expresses _intent_.

#### Use `:not()` instead of overrides to exclude irrelevant states/targets

When the intent is to exclude certain states or elements that are fundamentally irrelevant, use `:not()`.

For example, to apply bottom borders between list items, don't do this:

```css
.fancy-list li {
  border-bottom: 1px solid silver;
}

.fancy-list li:last-child {
  border-bottom: none;
}
```

This can unintentionally overwrite a desirable `border-bottom` set from another rule.
The actual intent was to only apply the bottom border to the non-last `li`s. The code above is a workaround that poorly expresses this intent. Instead, this expresses intent more clearly:

```css
.fancy-list li:not(:last-child) {
  border-bottom: 1px solid silver;
}
```

Similarly, don't do this:

```css
button:hover {
  background: var(--color-blue);
}

button:disabled {
  background: var(--color-neutral);
}
```

If we reorder the two rules, we will get a hover background on disabled buttons!
Instead, do this:

```css
button:hover:not(:disabled) {
  background: var(--color-blue);
}

button:disabled {
  background: var(--color-neutral);
}
```

This works regardless of reordering, as the first rule does not overmatch.

If you _must_ use an override (e.g. you are using an experimental container query and the `not` case is also the fallback), in some cases you may be able to use the `revert-layer` keyword to remove the value without coupling the override to specific values.
Note that this can only work if the value to fall back to is also layered.

#### Prefer `@scope` over `:not()` for excluding (potentially deeply nested) subtrees

While `:not()` + descendant selectors can exclude subtrees, this works poorly for deeply nested structures.
For example, `.card :not(.content *)` will not work as expected for nested cards.
`@scope` fixes this as it takes hierarchical proximity into account:

```css
@scope (.card) to (.content) {
  /* styles for elements inside .card but not inside .content */
}
```

This will work as expected even for nested cards.

#### Overrides are fine for specialization

This is fine:

```css
button {
  background: var(--color-neutral);
}

button.primary {
  background: var(--color-blue);
}
```

Both rules express legitimate _intent_: buttons are generally neutral, but primary ones are blue.

#### No global resets

**DO NOT** use global resets (styles on `*`) as they cannot be overridden by web components or lower-priority cascade layers (without `!important`). Instead, apply reset styles to specific element types and/or conditions.

### Nesting and scoping

Use native CSS nesting to group related styles to the extent it improves maintainability and readability.

Prefer `@scope` over nesting when proximity should matter more than pure specificity. This is common in selectors that can be nested in any order, but the closest matching one (in element -> ancestor order) should win, e.g. theming classes.

For example this will not work as expected:
```css
.dark .invert { color-scheme: light }
.light .invert { color-scheme: dark }
```

If `.invert` is nested within _both_ `.dark` and `.light`, it will always resolve to dark mode as both rules have the same specificity.
Using `@scope` fixes this:

```css
@scope (.dark) {
  .invert { color-scheme: light }
}

@scope (.light) {
  .invert { color-scheme: dark }
}
```

## 5. Design Tokens and Theming

Use CSS custom properties on `:root` to define core design variables (colors, fonts, sizes, etc) used throughout the design, for visual consistency and to scale UI design across teams.
**DO NOT** specify nontrivial styling values inline. E.g. `background: transparent` or `padding: 0` is ok, but `background: #f06` or `padding: .3em` are not.
One exception is use cases where keeping code small and simple is far more important than long-term maintainability and evolution, such as testcases.

Typically these are organized in tiers, with each tier building upon the previous one. For example:
1. Tier 1: Literal design tokens (e.g. `--color-blue-10`, `--color-gray-90`, `--font-sans-serif`, `--size-xl` etc)
2. Tier 2: Semantic design tokens (e.g. `--color-accent`, `--color-neutral`, `--font-body`, `--font-heading` etc)
3. Tier 3: General UI design tokens (e.g. `--ui-border`, `--surface-bg-subtle` etc)
4. Tier 4: Component-specific design tokens (e.g. `--button-bg-primary-hover`, `--button-border-color-secondary` etc)

The smaller the scope of the use case, the fewer tiers it needs. E.g. a quick demo or toy app are fine with one tier. Do not overengineer.
Check for any existing conventions around naming and levels before inventing your own.

# Build an address form that follows best practice

Create a form that makes it as easy as possible for users to enter address data on desktop and mobile. Ensure the form makes the most of built-in browser features for autofill, validation and data entry constraints.

## How to implement

Outlined below are the most important guidelines for building successful address forms.

### Use meaningful, valid HTML

Make the most of the elements and attributes built for creating forms:

-   `<form>`, `<input>`, `<label>`, and `<button>`
-   `type`, `autocomplete`, and `inputmode`

These enable built-in browser functionality, improve accessibility, and add meaning to markup.

### Use the `<label>` element to label form fields for data entry

To label an `<input>`, `<select>`, or `<textarea>`, use a `<label>`. Associate a label with an input by giving the label's `for` attribute the same value as the input's `id`.

### Make the most of HTML attributes

Make it easy for users to enter data, by using the appropriate `<input>` element with a `type` attribute to provide the right keyboard on mobile and enable basic built-in validation by the browser.

Always use `type="email"` for email addresses and `type="tel"` for phone numbers.

```html
<!-- type="email"/"tel" gives mobile users the right keyboard and enables built-in validation -->
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="email" required>
<input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone" autocomplete="tel">
```

Every `<input>`, `<select>`, and `<textarea>` element SHOULD have an appropriate `autocomplete` attribute, to improve accessibility and help users avoid re-entering data.

### Make buttons helpful

Use `<button>` for buttons. You can also use `<input type="submit">`, but don't use a `div` or some other random element acting as a button. Button elements provide accessible behaviour, built-in form submission functionality, and can easily be styled.

Give each form submit button a value that says what it does. For each step towards checkout, use a descriptive call-to-action that shows progress and makes the next step obvious. For example, label the submit button on your delivery address form **Proceed to Payment** rather than **Continue** or **Save**.

### Use a single name input where possible

Allow your users to enter their name using a single input, unless you have a good reason for separately storing given names, family names, honorifics, or other name parts. Using a single name input makes forms less complex, enables cut-and-paste, and makes autofill simpler. Use `autocomplete="name"` for a single input for name.

```html
<input type="text" id="fullname" name="fullname" autocomplete="name">
```

Allow international names. For validation, avoid using regular expressions that only match Latin characters. Latin-only excludes users with names or addresses that include characters that aren't in the Latin alphabet. Allow Unicode letter matching instead—and ensure your backend supports Unicode securely as both input and output. Unicode in regular expressions is well supported by modern browsers.

### Allow for a variety of address formats

When building an address form, be aware of the variety of address formats, even within a single country. Do not make assumptions about "normal" addresses.

Use a single `<textarea>` element for the street address if possible.

```html
<!-- textarea handles multi-line international address formats that split inputs can't accommodate -->
<textarea id="address" name="address" autocomplete="street-address" required></textarea>
```

This is the most flexible option for a variety of local and international address formats.

If your data model needs separate address lines, use one `<input>` per line with the `address-line1`, `address-line2` (and, if needed, `address-line3`) `autocomplete` tokens so that autofill still works. Don't split the street address across inputs that lack these tokens, and make only the first line required.

```html
<!-- Alternative: one input per line, each with its own autocomplete token -->
<input type="text" id="address-line1" name="address-line1" autocomplete="address-line1" required>
<input type="text" id="address-line2" name="address-line2" autocomplete="address-line2">
```

### Help save users from accidentally missing data fields

Add the `required` attribute to mandatory fields.

```html
<input type="text" id="city" name="city" autocomplete="address-level2" required>
```

### Fallback strategies

Baseline status for the html.elements.input.autocomplete capability: Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2015-07-29.
Supported by: Chrome 14 (Sep 2011), Edge 12 (Jul 2015), Firefox 4 (Mar 2011), and Safari 6 (Jul 2012).

Autofill is a progressive enhancement. In browsers that do not support autofill, users will simply need to manually enter their address details. The semantic HTML constraints (such as `type`, `inputmode`, and `required`) will still function appropriately as standard form validation.

# Build a sign-in form that follows best practice

Use cross-platform browser features to build sign-in forms that are secure, accessible and easy to use.

If users ever need to sign in to your site, then good sign-in form design is critical. This is especially true for people on poor connections, on mobile, in a hurry, or under stress. Poorly designed sign-in forms get high bounce rates. Each bounce could mean a lost customer and a disgruntled user—not just a missed sign-in opportunity.

## How to implement

Outlined below are the most important guidelines for building successful sign-in forms.

### Use meaningful, valid HTML

Make the most of the elements and attributes built for creating forms:

- `<form>`, `<input>`, `<label>`, and `<button>`
- `type`, `autocomplete`, and `inputmode`

These enable built-in browser functionality, improve accessibility, and add meaning to markup.

### Use the `<label>` element to label form fields for data entry

To label an `<input>`, `<select>`, or `<textarea>`, use a `<label>`. Associate a label with an input by giving the label's `for` attribute the same value as the input's `id`.

### Make the most of HTML attributes

Make it easy for users to enter data, by using the appropriate `<input>` element with a `type` attribute to provide the right keyboard on mobile and enable basic built-in validation by the browser.

Always use `type="email"` for email addresses and `type="tel"` for phone numbers.

Every `<input>`, `<select>`, and `<textarea>` element SHOULD have an appropriate `autocomplete` attribute, to improve accessibility and help users avoid re-entering data.

Username and email inputs hold identifiers, not prose. Add `spellcheck="false"` so the browser does not rewrite them into something the account does not match. `autocorrect` and `autocapitalize` are always disabled for `input type="email"`, but are required for non-email usernames.

### Make buttons helpful

Use `<button>` for buttons. You can also use `<input type="submit">`, but don't use a `div` or some other random element acting as a button. Button elements provide accessible behaviour, built-in form submission functionality, and can easily be styled.

Give each form submit button a value that says what it does. Use a clear, recognizable label. For example, use **Sign In** rather than **Continue** or **Submit**.

### Use a single name input where possible

Allow your users to enter their name using a single input, unless you have a good reason for separately storing given names, family names, honorifics, or other name parts. Using a single name input makes forms less complex, enables cut-and-paste, and makes autofill simpler. Use `autocomplete="name"` for a single input for name.

```html
<input type="text" id="fullname" name="fullname" autocomplete="name">
```

Allow international names. For validation, avoid using regular expressions that only match Latin characters. Latin-only excludes users with names or addresses that include characters that aren't in the Latin alphabet. Allow Unicode letter matching instead—and ensure your backend supports Unicode securely as both input and output. Unicode in regular expressions is well supported by modern browsers.

### Show sign-in progress

For each step towards sign-in, use page headings and descriptive button values that make it clear what needs to be done now, and what the next step is.

Use the `enterkeyhint` attribute on form inputs to set the mobile keyboard enter key label. For example, use `enterkeyhint="previous"` and `enterkeyhint="next"` within a multi-page form, `enterkeyhint="done"` for the final input in the form, and `enterkeyhint="search"` for a search input.

### Help users avoid re-entering sign-in data

Make sure to add appropriate `autocomplete` values in sign-in forms.

This enables browsers to help users by securely storing sign-in details and correctly entering form data. Without autocomplete, users may be more likely to keep a physical record of sign-in details, or store sign-in data insecurely on their device.

### Validate carefully

Validate data entry both in realtime and before form submission. Use `type="email"` for email inputs — the browser will validate the format automatically. Add the `required` attribute to mandatory fields to prevent empty submissions.

### Put sign-in in its own `<form>` element

Always use the `<form>` element when you're getting users to enter data

Don't wrap inputs in a `<div>` and handle input data submission purely with JavaScript. It's generally better to use a `<form>` element. This makes your site accessible to screen readers and other assistive devices, enables a range of built-in browser features, makes it simpler to build basic functional sign-in for older browsers, and can still work even if JavaScript fails.

### Don't double up inputs

Some sites force users to enter emails or passwords twice. That might reduce errors for a few users, but causes extra work for all users, and increases abandonment rates. Asking twice also makes no sense where browsers autofill email addresses or suggest strong passwords. It's better to enable users to confirm their email address (you'll need to do that anyway) and make it easy for them to reset their password if necessary.

### Keep passwords private—but enable users to see them if they want

Passwords inputs should have `type="password"` to hide password text and help the browser understand that the input is for passwords. (Note that browsers use a variety of techniques to understand input roles and decide whether or not to offer to save passwords.)

You should add a **Show password** toggle to enable users to check the text they've entered—and don't forget to add a **Forgot password** link.

### Give mobile users the right keyboard

Use `<input type="email">` to give mobile users an appropriate keyboard and enable basic built-in email address validation by the browser… no JavaScript required!

If you need to use a telephone number instead of an email address, `<input type="tel">` enables a telephone keypad on mobile. You can also use the `inputmode` attribute where necessary: `inputmode="numeric"` is ideal for PIN numbers.

### Prevent mobile keyboard from obstructing the Sign in button

If you're not careful, mobile keyboards may cover your form or, worse, partially obstruct the Sign in button. Users may give up before realizing what has happened.

Where possible, avoid this by displaying only the email (or phone) and password inputs and Sign in button at the top of your sign-in page. Put other content underneath.

### Help users to avoid re-entering data

You can help browsers store data correctly and autofill inputs, so users don't have to remember to enter email and password values. This is particularly important on mobile, and crucial for email inputs, which get high abandonment rates. There are two parts to this:

1.  The `autocomplete`, `name`, `id`, and `type` attributes help browsers understand the role of inputs in order to store data that can later be used for autofill. To allow data to be stored for autofill, modern browsers also require inputs to have a stable `name` or `id` value (not randomly generated on each page load or site deployment), and to be in a `<form>` element with a `submit` button.
1.  The `autocomplete` attribute helps browsers correctly autofill inputs using stored data.

For email inputs use `autocomplete="username"`, since `username` is recognized by password managers in modern browsers—even though you should use `type="email"` and you may want to use `id="email"` and `name="email"`. For password inputs, use the appropriate `autocomplete` value to help browsers differentiate between new and current passwords (`autocomplete="new-password"` and `autocomplete="current-password"` respectively).

### Use autocomplete="current-password" for an existing password

MANDATORY: Use `autocomplete="current-password"` for the password input in a sign-in form. This tells the browser that you want it to use the current password that it has stored for the site.

For a sign-in form:

```
<input type="password" autocomplete="current-password" id="current-password" …>
```

### Enable the browser to suggest a strong password

Modern browsers use heuristics to decide when to show the password manager UI and suggest a strong password.

Built-in browser password generators mean users and developers don't need to work out what a "strong password" is. Since browsers can securely store passwords and autofill them as necessary, there's no need for users to remember or enter passwords. Encouraging users to take advantage of built-in browser password generators also means they're more likely to use a unique, strong password on your site, and less likely to reuse a password that could be compromised elsewhere.

### Help save users from accidentally missing inputs

MANDATORY: Add the `required` attribute to both email and password fields. Modern browsers automatically prompt and set focus for missing data.

```html
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="username" required>
<input type="password" id="password" name="password" autocomplete="current-password" required>
```

### Allow password pasting

Some sites don't allow text to be pasted into password inputs.

Disallowing password pasting annoys users, encourages passwords that are memorable (and therefore may be easier to compromise) and, according to organizations such as the UK National Cyber Security Centre, may actually reduce security. Users only become aware that pasting is disallowed after they try to paste their password, so disallowing password pasting doesn't avoid clipboard vulnerabilities.
