Elsewhere the native `title` tooltip stays. MANDATORY: Position the hint on the axis the toolbar does not stack along: `position-area: block-end` (fallback `flip-block`) for a horizontal toolbar, `position-area: inline-end` (fallback `flip-inline`) for a vertical one. A hint placed along the stacking axis covers the next control and swallows its click, because the hint stays open while the pointer is over it. ```html ``` ```js // Upgrade title tooltips only when interest invokers and anchor positioning both work if ("interestForElement" in HTMLButtonElement.prototype && CSS.supports("position-area", "block-end")) { document.querySelectorAll('[role="toolbar"] button[title]').forEach((b, i) => { const tip = Object.assign(document.createElement("div"), { id: `tip-${i}`, textContent: b.title }); tip.popover = "hint"; b.setAttribute("interestfor", tip.id); b.removeAttribute("title"); // avoid a second, native tooltip document.body.append(tip); // keep open hint nodes out of role="group" / role="toolbar" }); } ``` `interestfor` is specified to wire hint popovers (`popover="hint"`) for assistive technology itself, based on what the target contains. A **plain hint** (text and images only) becomes the trigger's accessible description, or its name if it has none. A **rich hint** (headings, links, or other interactive content) gets a minimum role of `tooltip`, the trigger gets `aria-expanded` and an `aria-details` relation while the hint is open, and the open hint comes right after the trigger in the tab order so keyboard users can reach its content. Browsers and screen readers do not yet expose this consistently, so add explicit ARIA as well: - **Hint that repeats the trigger's accessible name** (e.g. an icon-only button with `aria-label="Bold"` and a "Bold" tooltip): add nothing. A description identical to the name would be read twice. - **Hint on a trigger with no visible label of its own** (e.g. an icon-only button without `aria-label`): `aria-labelledby` on the trigger pointing at the hint, so the hint becomes the name. - **Hint whose trigger also opens it on activation** (a toggletip, or any button whose only job is the hint: give it `popovertarget` with `popovertargetaction="show"`): `role="tooltip"` on the hint and `aria-expanded` on the trigger, kept in sync with the popover's `toggle` event. A description read right after "button" suggests further actions and muddles the role; the expanded state tells the user there is content to reveal and whether it is open, and pressing the button delivers it. Place the hint right after the trigger in the DOM so reading keys reach its content once it is open. - **Hint whose trigger does something else on activation** (a link, a button with its own action): `role="tooltip"` on the hint and `aria-describedby` on the trigger, never `aria-expanded`. A trigger announced as "collapsed" suggests `Enter` would expand it, but `Enter` navigates or acts. The hint must be something the user can afford to miss: a hovercard previews the destination, a tooltip on an action button describes the action. - **DO NOT** attach a hint that opens on activation to a control that already uses `aria-expanded` for something else (for example, a menu button). Give that hint its own trigger instead. - **DO NOT** move focus into the target when interest is shown (no `autofocus`, no `focus()` in an `interest` listener). Interest is triggered by hover or focus alone, so moving focus would fail WCAG 3.2.1 (On Focus). Not every screen reader reads descriptions when moving through the page (NVDA skips them in browse mode by design), so a hint exposed as a description must only carry content the user can afford to miss. Link previews and tooltips on action controls qualify; anything the user needs belongs in a toggletip or inline. Wire this with a short script instead of hand-authoring the attributes, so the markup stays declarative and the same rules apply to every hint. The script should: 1. Run in every browser, before loading the `interestfor` polyfill, once the DOM is parsed, and expose a function that can be called again for content inserted later. Scanning upfront is required: a browse-mode screen reader user needs the attributes in place before any interaction, so wiring them lazily on `focus` or `interest` is too late, and so is waiting for the polyfill, which wires its ARIA only on `load` and adds no `role="tooltip"` to plain hints. 2. For every `[interestfor]` trigger whose target has `popover="hint"`, normalize whitespace and compare the hint text with the trigger's accessible name (`aria-labelledby` targets, else `aria-label`, else text content including image `alt`, else `title`). Equal: do nothing. Otherwise set `role="tooltip"` on the hint if it has no role. 3. When the trigger has no name, point `aria-labelledby` at the hint unless it already has one. Otherwise, if the trigger also opens the hint on activation (a `popovertarget` or `commandfor` naming the hint), set `aria-expanded` to the popover's current state (`:popover-open`) unless it already has `aria-expanded`, and remember which triggers the script owns; if not, point `aria-describedby` at the hint unless it already has one. 4. Keep `aria-expanded` in sync from the popover's `toggle` event in every browser with a single capturing listener on `document`, updating every trigger with a matching `interestfor` that the script owns (the `interestfor` polyfill does not sync `aria-expanded` on plain-text hints or when a toggletip is opened via `popovertarget`). Things that are easy to get wrong: - `toggle` does not bubble. A bubbling listener on `document` never fires; use the capture phase (or a listener per popover). - Sync `aria-expanded` from `toggle`, not from `interest`/`loseinterest`. The popover is the source of truth: it can be closed by `Escape`, light dismiss, or another invoker, and several triggers can share one hint. - A hidden popover is a valid `aria-describedby` or `aria-labelledby` target. Do not force the hint open or duplicate its text to make it "visible". - Do not add `aria-haspopup` or a live region to any hint. - Do not override author ARIA: an existing `aria-describedby`, `aria-labelledby`, or `aria-expanded` on the trigger wins. By default, interest is shown and lost for keyboard and mouse users with a delay of half a second. This prevents the targeted popover from opening while tabbing through a page or moving your mouse around, and from closing while moving your mouse from the trigger to the popover. To adjust the timing, use the `interest-delay` CSS property. ```css [interestfor]{ /* Shorthand for interest-delay-start and interest-delay-end */ interest-delay: 0.2s 0.1s; } ``` If users are likely to move through multiple triggers in quick succession, set the initial delay to `0s` if an interest-triggered popover is already open. ```css :root:has(:interest-source) [interestfor] { interest-delay-start: 0s; } ``` ```css [popover="hint"] { inset: auto; /* Anchor to the invoker; flip to the other side if there is no room */ position-area: block-end; position-try-fallbacks: flip-block; } ``` ## Overflow menu for secondary actions (optional) Two patterns fit a toolbar into a narrow space: an overflow menu, better on desktop, or a horizontally scrollable toolbar with no scrollbar and scroll hints, better on mobile. For the scrollable pattern use `overflow-x: auto; scrollbar-width: none; scroll-snap-type: x proximity`, and hint at hidden controls with edge fades (`mask-image`) or a partly visible last item. Choose by input type (`@media (pointer: coarse)`) or container width. Add a trailing "More actions" menu when the toolbar has secondary actions or must fit narrow containers; skip it if every control is common and fits. If items must move into the menu dynamically as space runs out, build that overflow behavior yourself. * Make the trigger the last toolbar item (`aria-label="More actions"`, `aria-haspopup="menu"`, `aria-expanded="false"`, and `popovertarget` pointing at the menu popover) with the conventional three vertical dots icon (`⋮`). Open it only on activation—never preview on focus when arrowing across the toolbar. * Anchor the `popover` container to its trigger (`inset: auto; position-area: block-end span-inline-start; position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline`) and nest `
` inside it, adding `role="menu"`, `role="menuitem"`, `tabindex="-1"`, and `ArrowDown`/`ArrowUp`/`Home`/`End` only when `'focusGroup' in HTMLElement.prototype` is false. Sync `aria-expanded` and focus the first item on `toggle`, close the popover on `Tab` without trapping focus, and let `Space` on `role="menuitemcheckbox"` toggle `aria-checked` without closing. For nested submenus or radio groups, see `menu` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "menu"`). * Announce the result of every menu activation in the toolbar's live region, such as `"Strikethrough on"` or `"Formatting cleared"`. When closing the menu returns focus to the trigger, delay the live-region write slightly—for example `500ms`—so the focus-change announcement does not preempt it. ## Fallback strategies ### Fallbacks & browser support for `focusgroup` Browser support for focusgroup: Limited availability. Supported by: Chrome 150 (Jun 2026) and Edge 150 (Jul 2026). Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari. Keep `focusgroup` in the markup. Only if `'focusGroup' in HTMLElement.prototype` is false, load a roving-tabindex fallback; never install it when native focusgroup is present. The fallback implements what focusgroup does natively: * The active item has `tabindex="0"`; all others have `tabindex="-1"`. Initially the first item is active. * On `focusin`, move `tabindex="0"` to the focused item so returning to the toolbar (including after a click) restores position. * In a horizontal toolbar, `ArrowRight`/`ArrowLeft` move to the next/previous item across all groups and wrap at the ends. In RTL, reverse the directions. Do not wire `ArrowUp`/`ArrowDown`. * In a vertical toolbar, `ArrowDown`/`ArrowUp` move to the next/previous item instead, and `ArrowLeft`/`ArrowRight` do nothing. * `Home`/`End` move to the first/last item. * Call `preventDefault()` only for keys the toolbar handles so `Tab` keeps working. ```js if (!('focusGroup' in HTMLElement.prototype)) { // items = every toolbar control across all groups, in DOM order items.forEach((b, i) => (b.tabIndex = i ? -1 : 0)); bar.addEventListener("focusin", ({ target }) => { if (items.includes(target)) items.forEach((b) => (b.tabIndex = b === target ? 0 : -1)); }); // Read direction and orientation at event time so runtime changes are honored const vertical = bar.getAttribute("aria-orientation") === "vertical"; // Only horizontal toolbars flip with direction: RTL does not flip Up/Down const rtl = getComputedStyle(bar).direction === "rtl"; const steps = vertical ? { ArrowDown: 1, ArrowUp: -1 } : { ArrowRight: rtl ? -1 : 1, ArrowLeft: rtl ? 1 : -1 }; // keydown: look up steps[key] (or Home/End), move focus, preventDefault only for handled keys } ``` ### Fallbacks & browser support for Interest invokers Browser support for Interest invokers: Limited availability. Supported by: Chrome 149 (Jun 2026) and Edge 149 (Jun 2026). Unsupported in: Firefox and Safari. Do not load an `interestfor` polyfill here: when native interest invokers or anchor positioning are missing, the upgrade script is skipped and buttons keep their baseline `title` tooltip. ### Fallbacks & browser support for Popover Baseline status for Popover: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2025-01-27. Supported by: Chrome 116 (Aug 2023), Edge 116 (Aug 2023), Firefox 125 (Apr 2024), Safari 17 (Sep 2023), and Safari iOS 18.3 (Jan 2025). The Popover API is mostly **progressive enhancement**, but its defining behaviors — top-layer promotion, light-dismiss, and `popovertarget` invocation — have no CSS-only equivalent. Older browsers need a polyfill, or a manual fallback if you would rather not ship one. **Polyfill:** To support the `popover` attribute in older browsers, conditionally load [`@oddbird/popover-polyfill`](https://github.com/oddbird/popover-polyfill). **MANDATORY:** Feature detect by checking for the `popover` property on `HTMLElement.prototype`, and load the polyfill **only** when native support is missing — do NOT load it unconditionally. With a bundler or import map: ```js // MANDATORY: Feature detect 'popover' on HTMLElement.prototype. if (!Object.hasOwn(HTMLElement.prototype, "popover")) { import("@oddbird/popover-polyfill"); } ``` If not using a package manager, import from a CDN, e.g. `"https://unpkg.com/@oddbird/popover-polyfill@latest/dist/popover.min.js"`. Caveats when using the polyfill: - Do NOT use the `popover` IDL attribute for any code that may run before the polyfill is fully loaded. It will not be mirrored as an attribute, the popover will not be picked up by the polyfill, and the property will be shadowing the accessor the polyfill adds forever. Use `setAttribute()`/`removeAttribute()` instead. - **Styling caveat:** The polyfill cannot define the real `:popover-open` pseudo-class, so it applies a `.\:popover-open` class instead. **MANDATORY:** Combine the two with `:is()` or `:where()`, otherwise browsers that lack `:popover-open` discard the entire rule: ```css [popover]:is(:popover-open, .\:popover-open) { display: block; } ``` ### Fallbacks & browser support for `popover="hint"` Browser support for popover="hint": Limited availability. Supported by: Chrome 151 (Jul 2026), Edge 151 (Jul 2026), and Firefox 153 (Jul 2026). Unsupported in: Safari. The popover polyfill does not add `popover="hint"`. Where `popover` exists without `hint`, two tooltips can stay open at once (for example one opened by focus and one by hover). Treat this as graceful degradation: the upgrade only runs where interest invokers are supported, and other browsers keep the native `title` tooltip. ### Fallbacks & browser support for Clipboard API Baseline status for the api.Clipboard.writeText capability: Widely available. It's been Baseline since 2020-03-24. Supported by: Chrome 66 (Apr 2018), Edge 79 (Jan 2020), Firefox 63 (Oct 2018), Safari 13.1 (Mar 2020), and Safari iOS 13.4 (Mar 2020). Where the Clipboard API is unavailable, `navigator.clipboard` is undefined and the call throws, so the `catch` branch in the feedback snippet reports the failure. ### Fallbacks & browser support for Anchor positioning Browser support for Anchor positioning: Limited availability. Supported by: Safari 27 (Sep 2026). Unsupported in: Chrome, Edge, and Firefox. Without anchor positioning, a popover is placed by the UA at the center of the viewport. Tooltips need no fallback: the `title` upgrade above is skipped without anchor positioning. For the overflow menu, position it from script so it stays attached to its trigger. Keep the CSS inside `@supports not (position-area: block-end)` so supporting browsers are unaffected. ```css @supports not (position-area: block-end) { #more-menu { /* Viewport coordinates are set from script when the menu opens */ position: fixed; inset: auto; margin: 0; } } ``` ```js // Only needed without anchor positioning; place the menu below its trigger // and flip above it when it would overflow the viewport. menu.addEventListener("toggle", ({ newState }) => { if (newState !== "open" || CSS.supports("position-area", "block-end")) return; const t = more.getBoundingClientRect(); const m = menu.getBoundingClientRect(); const below = t.bottom + m.height <= innerHeight; menu.style.top = `${below ? t.bottom : t.top - m.height}px`; // Right-align with the trigger, clamped to the viewport menu.style.left = `${Math.max(0, Math.min(t.right - m.width, innerWidth - m.width))}px`; }); ```

# Theming browser-generated UI

Most browser-generated UI can be customized to some extent using CSS.
Even if it requires modern features, it degrades gracefully in older browsers, and thus often does not require a polyfill or fallback.

Before re-creating browser UI (form controls, scrollbars, selections, error messages, etc), first verify that:
1. the browser UI cannot be customized enough for your needs, even with modern CSS,
2. the desired customization is sufficiently critical to justify the tradeoffs of re-creating built-in UI — most notably losing accessible semantics, keyboard handling, IME, and AT integration that the native UI provides for free.

Example customizations that are possible:
- Use `::selection` to customize highlighted text colors.
- **DON'T** apply `user-select: none` to content text — breaks copy-paste, translation tools, and AT "read from here" gestures. Limit it to chrome (drag handles, toolbars, redundant button labels).
- Use `accent-color` to apply the page's accent color to any browser-generated UI.
- Use `color-scheme` to have browser UI adapt to light/dark mode.
- Use `scrollbar-color` to customize scrollbar colors — keep the thumb visibly distinct from the track (contrast ≥3:1)
- **DON'T** use the `scrollbar-width` with any value other than `auto`, unless another accessible option is provided to scroll content. Although `scrollbar-width: thin` does provide a thumb, the target size of the thumb will be too small for some users to operate.
- Use `:user-invalid` / `:user-valid` for validity styling, **not** `:invalid` / `:valid` — they only match after the user has interacted with the field, avoiding the hostile default of flagging required-empty fields as errors on page load. Exclude range sliders when targeting `input` broadly (e.g., `input:not(input[type="range"]):user-valid`) so adjusting a slider does not apply field validity borders or backgrounds to it.
- Buttons and text fields (including `<textarea>`) can generally be styled as normal elements.
- Use `font-size` to scale and other textual properties to control typography
- Use text color contrast between the foreground and background colors of at least 4.5:1 for regular size text or at least `3:1` for large-scale text (18 point or 14 point bold font size).
- Use a contrast between adjacent colors of at least `3:1` for non-text content.

### Styling textual fields (`<input>` & `<textarea>`)

For most styling purposes (e.g. colors, borders, backgrounds, typography, etc) treat these elements as normal text containers.

- Use `:placeholder-shown` and `::placeholder` to style input placeholders.
- Use `field-sizing: content` to make text fields size to content.
- For `<textarea>` elements, use `resize: vertical` to disable horizontal resizing.
- Do not use `resize: none` on `<textarea>` elements to disable all resizing, without an alternative resizing mechanism, such as using `field-sizing: content;` or providing custom resize buttons.

### Multiple choice controls (select, radios, checkboxes)

- To select one among many options presented in a dropdown: Use a `<select>` + `appearance: base-select` + `::picker(select)`. For more info see `branded-select-styling` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "branded-select-styling"`)
- Selecting one or more among multiple options laid out inline in the page: Use a `<input type=checkbox>` or `<input type=radio>` inside a `<label>` for each option. Style via `label:has(:checked)`.
- Style checkboxes, radios and switches via `appearance: none` + generated content (`::before`/`::after`) or background images to draw the checked state.
<!-- Customizable select listbox version currently buggy + this has much better browser support -->

### Non-textual `<input>`s (buttons, sliders, file inputs etc.)

- File inputs: Use `::file-selector-button` to style the button.
- Do not use `<input>` with a `type` of `button`, `submit` or `reset`. Use `<button>` instead and style it as a regular element.
- Sliders: Use `appearance: none` + thumb pseudo-elements (`::-webkit-slider-thumb`, `::-moz-range-thumb`, etc) and track pseudo-elements (`::-webkit-slider-runnable-track`, `::-moz-range-track`, etc) for more granular control.

# Color ## Accessible color **Don't use color alone to indicate the presence of a user interface component or its state**: Use iconography and/or shape to help differentiate. Do not denote success/errors ONLY with color. Use icons or text (WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color). ```html
❌ The password entered was invalid.
``` ### Contrast - **Minimum contrast standards**: Maintain 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (at least 24px, or at least 18.66px bold) or icons (WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) for text, WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast for icons). - **Ensure non-text contrast standards**: Maintain a minimum contrast ratio of 3:1 for user interface component boundaries and states (WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast). - This includes visual elements (borders, backgrounds, box-shadows, underlines) that form the boundary or indicate the presence of a UI component (e.g., input field borders). - This also includes visual elements indicating active states within a component (e.g., checkbox checkmarks, switch thumbs or custom focus indicators). - **Caveat**: Meeting 3:1 non-text contrast can challenge minimalistic designs. Soft gradients or subtle inset/outset shadows can soften visual boundaries while satisfying accessibility requirements. - **Use `prefers-contrast` only when warranted**: Reach for `@media (prefers-contrast: more)` when the design uses low-contrast accents (e.g., subtle borders, muted secondary text) that need to be reinforced; most sites that already meet baseline contrast won't need it. It strengthens colors that already meet the minimums above; it doesn't fix a default that fails them, because it only reaches users who have turned on the setting. ### Light and dark color schemes - **Support light and dark color schemes**: Honor `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` and pair it with the `color-scheme` CSS property so form controls, scrollbars, and other UA-rendered surfaces match. See `dark-mode` (via `npx -y modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "dark-mode"`) for more details. ### Forced Colors Mode - **Support Forced Colors Mode**: In Forced Colors Mode (High Contrast on Windows), the browser overrides author colors with system keywords, removes `box-shadow`, `text-shadow`, and gradient backgrounds, and may also remove `border-image`. `url()` background images can't be relied on either: they may be removed, or kept in their own colors, which may not contrast with the system colors. Define system color fallbacks for color tokens using `@media (forced-colors: active)`. - **Use `forced-color-adjust: none` only where color is essential information** (syntax highlighter, color picker swatch). **DON'T** use `forced-color-adjust: none` just to preserve aesthetics. Where the element contains text, set both its text and background colors to a pair that meets the minimums above, because a transparent background shows what is behind it, usually the user's system `Canvas` color, which can be light or dark. - **Don't rely on `background-image`, `box-shadow`, or `border-image` to convey borders, separators, or state**: In forced colors they disappear or keep their own colors, which may not contrast with the system colors (and they often disappear in print too). If you must, ensure there's an alternative in forced colors mode, such as `outline` or `border` with system color keywords (`CanvasText`, `LinkText`, `ButtonText`, `Highlight`, `GrayText`, etc.). ## Generating tints Before generating tints dynamically, check if you can use an existing, predefined, design token. This allows much more designer control and ensures consistency. If you need to generate lighter or darker colors dynamically: - **DO NOT** just adjust the lightness channel in `oklch`/`oklab` or `lch`/`lab`, e.g. `oklab(from var(--primary) 0.9 a b)`. While that is theoretically the correct way, browsers do not yet implement gamut mapping, so the resulting color is unpredictable. - You can use `color-mix()` to mix with white or black (preferably in `oklab`). This keeps the color safely in gamut, but tends to over-desaturate colors and produce washed out tints and shades. - You MAY combine lightness adjustment with any of the other methods (e.g. `color-mix(in oklab, oklch(from var(--primary) 0.9 c h), white 30%)`) for a balance between the two, but avoid going above 30% for the lightness adjustment.

# Improve Text Layout and Legibility The layout of text, particularly at the ends of lines and ends of paragraphs, can impact the legibility and aesthetic appeal of a page. CSS provides several text wrapping options that can improve specific use cases. For short text blocks like headings, use `text-wrap: balance`. This property instructs the browser to distribute text as evenly as possible across lines, creating a more symmetrical appearance. The `text-wrap: pretty` CSS property allows you to improve the typographic quality of body text by enabling a more sophisticated wrapping algorithm. It is specifically designed to prevent "orphans" (single words on the last line of a paragraph) and create a more pleasing visual "rag" for long blocks of text. ## Implementation ### 1. **Identify text elements**: For `text-wrap: balance`, select short text blocks like headings and table headers. Avoid elements that have visible boxes such as borders or backgrounds, as this can create unexpected visually empty areas in the layout. For `text-wrap: pretty`, select elements potentially containing long runs of text where orphaned words (runts) or poor line breaks are most noticeable. This includes the following elements: - `

` - `

` - `
  • ` - Any other element potentially containing long runs of text. #### Choosing the Right Wrapping Method | Criteria | `text-wrap: balance` | `text-wrap: pretty` | `text-wrap: wrap` (Default) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Best For** | Short blocks (Headings, Titles) | Long blocks (Paragraphs, Lists) | Performance-critical content | | **Visual Goal** | Symmetrical line lengths | Avoiding orphans ("runts") | Fast, standard wrapping | | **Line Constraints** | Up to 6–10 lines (algorithm limit) | Best for 3 to many lines | No limit | | **Perf Cost** | **High**: Binary search algorithm | **Medium**: Look-back algorithm | **Low**: Standard greedy algorithm | ### 2. **Apply the chosen wrapping**: Apply `text-wrap: balance` specifically to short, multi-line elements such as headings (`h1`-`h6`), subheadings, or pullquotes. ```css /* Target specific heading elements for balanced wrapping */ h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6 { /* Enables balanced line-breaking logic */ text-wrap: balance; } ``` Use `text-wrap: pretty` to enable an optimized algorithm that evaluates the last few lines of a paragraph to find the best break points. ```css /* Apply to multi-line text blocks to prevent orphaned words */ p, blockquote, li, .pretty-text { /* Enables pretty line-breaking logic for body copy */ text-wrap: pretty; } ``` ### Critical Constraints and Performance #### text-wrap: balance * **Line Limit:** Browsers impose a limit on the number of lines they will attempt to balance to maintain performance (typically **6 lines** in Chromium and **10 lines** in Firefox). If the text exceeds this limit, the browser reverts to standard `wrap` behavior. Avoid using `text-wrap: balance` on text blocks that are likely to exceed these limits. * **Targeted Application:** DO NOT apply `text-wrap: balance` globally (e.g., `* { text-wrap: balance; }`). The iterative "binary search" algorithm used by browsers is computationally expensive. Limit its use to specific, short text elements. * **Interaction with Width:** `text-wrap: balance` does not change the container's width (`inline-size`). It only affects how text wraps *within* that width. This can leave empty space at the end of the container, which may affect layouts relying on full-width text blocks. #### text-wrap: pretty * **Performance vs. Quality**: MANDATORY: `text-wrap: pretty` is more computationally expensive than the default `wrap` (greedy) algorithm because it evaluates multiple lines (typically the last four) to optimize the break points. Avoid applying it globally to every element if your page has an extreme amount of text content. * **Best for multi-line text**: The benefits of `pretty` are most apparent in paragraphs of three or more lines. It has little to no effect on short, single-line text. * **Browser-specific behavior**: Be aware that implementation details vary. Chromium-based browsers typically focus on the last four lines, while other engines may evaluate the entire paragraph. ### Fallback strategies Baseline status for text-wrap: balance: Newly available. It's been Baseline since 2024-05-13. Supported by: Chrome 114 (May 2023), Edge 114 (Jun 2023), Firefox 121 (Dec 2023), and Safari 17.5 (May 2024). Browser support for text-wrap: pretty: Limited availability. Supported by: Chrome 117 (Sep 2023), Edge 117 (Sep 2023), and Safari 26 (Sep 2025). Unsupported in: Firefox. In browsers that do not support `text-wrap: balance` or `text-wrap: pretty`, the property is ignored, and the text will wrap using the default `wrap` behavior. This is a progressive enhancement that gracefully degrades to standard typography. This ensures that your content remains perfectly readable across all browsers while providing a superior experience to those that support it. For critical layouts where refined text layout is a requirement, use a JavaScript library, but be aware that this may be slow and cause performance issues.

# Typography

## Overall best practices

- Use unitless numbers for `line-height` (e.g., `1.5`) to ensure relative scaling during font-size inheritance.
- Use `overflow-wrap: break-word` (or `anywhere`) to contain long URLs.
- **DON'T** use `px` for font-size. Prefer `rem` to honor the user's browser font-size preferences (root font size), or `em`/percentages for contextual sizing.
- **DON'T** set a fixed `height` or `block-size` on elements that contain text, such as buttons, badges, tabs and cards. Let the content set the height, with `min-block-size` if a minimum is needed, so text doesn't overflow or get clipped when users increase text spacing to a line height of 1.5, spacing after paragraphs of 2em, letter spacing of 0.12em and word spacing of 0.16em (WCAG 1.4.12 Text Spacing requires no loss of content or functionality at these values).

## Readability

- **Avoid long lines of text**: Cap paragraph blocks to a maximum of 80 characters width.
- **Avoid rivers of whitespace**: Avoid `text-align: justify` as it can make text harder to read. If you must use it, combine it with `hyphens: auto` to avoid excessive whitespace between words. `hyphens: auto` only hyphenates text whose language is declared with the `lang` attribute, such as `<html lang="en">`.
- **Don't use Ornate fonts**: Omit cursive typefaces for main reading content.
- **Don't rely on all-caps for emphasis**: Prefer bolding for visual emphasis, and use `<em>`/`<strong>` when the emphasis is semantic.
- **Limit emphasis overall**: Emphasis loses meaning when it's everywhere — apply it only where it changes how the content should be read.
- **Support user zoom preferences**: Allow users to resize text up to 200% without loss of content or functionality, and let text reflow at a 320 CSS px viewport width without horizontal scrolling (WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow); avoid `white-space: nowrap` and fixed widths on running text.

```css
body {
  line-height: 1.5;
  text-align: start; /* Supports LTR and RTL */
}
article {
  max-width: 60ch; /* Caps line length to ~80 characters for readability (1ch is the width of "0", which is wider than most characters) */
}
```

## Text wrapping

- Use `text-wrap: balance` for balanced headlines and headline-like content (e.g. `<th>`)
- Use `text-wrap: pretty` for long-form body text (paragraphs, blockquotes, etc.)
- Use `text-wrap: balance` or `text-wrap: pretty` deliberately, **DO NOT** apply it on `*` as it does have a performance cost.
- Avoid `text-wrap: balance` on elements with a visible box (backgrounds, borders, shadows, etc) as it does not change the container's width, it only affects how text wraps *within* that width. This can leave empty space at the end of the container, which is usually undesirable.

## Responsive Typography

- **DO** combine viewport-relative and font-relative units in `clamp()` for font sizes that scale with the viewport size while ensuring they stay within a desired range. For example, `clamp(2rem, 1rem + 5vw, 4rem)`. Adjust the proportion of viewport-relative and font-relative units to control how quickly the font-size changes. Use font-relative minimum and maximum values, and keep the maximum no more than 2.5 times the minimum. Viewport units don't grow when users zoom, so the text only grows once its minimum overtakes the viewport-based value; with a maximum no more than 2.5 times the minimum, browser zoom, which goes up to 500%, can still resize the text to 200% (WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text requires text to resize up to 200% without loss of content or functionality).
- **DON'T** use `vw` alone for font-size without `clamp()`, as it can scale text too small or too large on extreme screens.

# Compiling C and C++ to WebAssembly with Emscripten

Use Emscripten (`emcc` and `em++`) to compile C and C++ into high-performance
WebAssembly (Wasm) modules for the browser.

## 1. Recommended Emscripten Compilation Flags

When compiling and linking with `emcc` or `em++`, use modern modular flags:

- `-sSTRICT`: Opt into strict modern Emscripten behavior and disable deprecated
  or legacy compatibility features.
- `-sEXPORT_ES6`: Emit a standard ES6 module (`import`/`export`). This option
  automatically implies `-sMODULARIZE`, encapsulating generated code so it does
  not pollute the global namespace.
- `-sENVIRONMENT=web` (or `-sENVIRONMENT=worker` when running solely inside a
  Web Worker, or `-sENVIRONMENT=web,worker` for both): Strip Node.js and shell
  runtime support code to minimize bundle size.
- `-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH`: Allow the WebAssembly linear memory heap to expand
  dynamically when allocations exceed the initial heap size.
- `-Werror -Wall`: Treat compiler warnings as errors to catch C/C++ bugs and
  invalid compiler settings early.
- `-O3`, `-Os`, or `-Oz` with `-flto`: In release builds, choose `-O3` when
  runtime performance is most critical, or `-Os` / `-Oz` when minimizing binary
  payload size is the priority. Pass `-flto` during both compilation and
  linking for Link-Time Optimization.

### Command-Line Style

Keep `emcc` and `em++` invocations clean, minimal, and consistent:

- **Omit settings that are enabled by default**: Do not pass redundant flags
  that are already default in modern Emscripten, such as `-sWASM`, or
  `-sMODULARIZE` when `-sEXPORT_ES6` is already specified.
- **Omit the `=1` suffix on boolean `-s` flags**: Write `-sSTRICT`,
  `-sEXPORT_ES6`, and `-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH` rather than `-sSTRICT=1`,
  `-sEXPORT_ES6=1`, or `-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1`.
- **Prefer standard compiler flags over Emscripten-specific ones**: Use
  `-pthread` instead of `-sUSE_PTHREADS`, and `-m64` instead of `-sMEMORY64`.
- **Use simple comma-separated lists**: For list-based settings, pass
  comma-separated values without brackets or quotes (for example,
  `-sEXPORTED_FUNCTIONS=_render,_malloc,_free` and
  `-sEXPORTED_RUNTIME_METHODS=HEAPU8`) rather than JSON arrays like
  `-sEXPORTED_FUNCTIONS=['_render','_malloc','_free']`.
- **Use response files for long lists**: If an export list is large, pass a
  response file (`@filename`) instead of a long inline list (for example,
  `-sEXPORTED_FUNCTIONS=@exported_funcs.txt`).
- **Use separate compilation for multi-file projects**: Compile `.c` / `.cpp`
  sources to `.o` object files (`em++ -c`) before linking them into the final
  module rather than combining everything into a single monolithic invocation.

```bash
# Compile C++ source to an object file
em++ -c renderer.cpp -o renderer.o -O3 -flto -Werror -Wall

# Link into an ES6 WebAssembly module targeting a Web Worker
em++ renderer.o -o renderer.js \
  -O3 -flto \
  -sSTRICT \
  -sEXPORT_ES6 \
  -sENVIRONMENT=worker \
  -sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH \
  -sEXPORTED_FUNCTIONS=_render_frame,_malloc,_free \
  -sEXPORTED_RUNTIME_METHODS=HEAPU8
```

### Debug vs. Release Profiles

Keep compile and link flags consistent within each build profile, and never
ship debug information in production:

- **Release builds**: Use `-O3`, `-Os`, or `-Oz` combined with `-flto` on both
  compile and link steps, and omit `-g` and `-sASSERTIONS`. Add `--closure=1`
  when linking to minify the generated JavaScript glue code unless an external
  bundler already minifies it.
- **Debug builds**: Use `-g` when compiling and `-g`, `-gline-tables-only`, or
  `-gsource-map` when linking, alongside `-sASSERTIONS`. Avoid optimization
  flags (`-O2`, `-O3`, `-Os`, `-Oz`) and `-flto` in debug builds for faster
  compilation and accurate source-level debugging.

## 2. JavaScript-WebAssembly Boundary Efficiency

Avoid high-frequency calls across the JavaScript-WebAssembly boundary. Calling
an exported Wasm function per pixel, per audio sample, or per vertex incurs
boundary overhead that negates Wasm performance gains.

Instead, design C/C++ entry points to process entire buffers or memory regions
in a single call and read or write the contiguous buffer in linear memory:

```js
import initRenderer from './renderer.js';

const wasm = await initRenderer();
const byteLength = width * height * 4;
const ptr = wasm._malloc(byteLength);

try {
  wasm._render_frame(ptr, width, height, samples);
  const pixels = new Uint8ClampedArray(
    wasm.HEAPU8.buffer,
    ptr,
    byteLength,
  ).slice();
  self.postMessage({ pixels, width, height }, [pixels.buffer]);
} finally {
  wasm._free(ptr);
}
```

Note: Accessing `wasm.HEAPU8.buffer` directly after calls that may grow memory
requires reading `wasm.HEAPU8` fresh after the Wasm call returns, because
`-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH` detaches the previous `ArrayBuffer` when resizing.

## 3. Avoid Blocking the Main Thread

The browser relies on cooperative multitasking on the main UI thread. Any
WebAssembly call that takes more than a few milliseconds (such as image
rendering, ray tracing, physics simulation, or heavy parsing) **must not** run
synchronously on the main thread, or it will freeze page rendering and input.

Use one of these approaches to keep the UI responsive:

1. **Run the WebAssembly module in a Web Worker**: Instantiate and call the
   ES6 Wasm module inside a dedicated module Worker
   (`new Worker(new URL('./worker.js', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' })`),
   and pass rendered buffers back via `postMessage` with transferable
   `ArrayBuffer` objects.
2. **Use multithreading (`-pthread`)**: Offload heavy compute across background
   workers using standard POSIX threads. Note that `-pthread` requires
   `SharedArrayBuffer`, which requires serving the page in a cross-origin
   isolated context (`Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and
   `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`).
3. **Yield to the browser event loop**: Restructure continuous loops in C/C++
   to run one frame at a time via `emscripten_set_main_loop`, or use
   JavaScript Promise Integration (`-sJSPI`) / Asyncify (`-sASYNCIFY`) when
   synchronous C/C++ code must pause for asynchronous JavaScript APIs.

## 4. Test Runtime Execution and Memory Limits

Always run and verify the compiled WebAssembly module in a real browser
environment and confirm that no warnings or unhandled errors appear in the
console:

- **Validate with `-sASSERTIONS` during development**: Build and test with
  `-sASSERTIONS` enabled to catch invalid memory accesses, missing exports, or
  ABI mismatches early, then remove `-sASSERTIONS` for the final release build.
- **Watch for stack overflows in recursive C/C++ code**: Emscripten's default
  execution stack size (`-sSTACK_SIZE`) is 64 KB, which is much smaller than
  native OS stacks. Deeply recursive algorithms (such as recursive ray tracers
  or tree traversals) can overflow the stack and corrupt linear memory unless
  converted to an iterative loop or linked with a larger stack (for example,
  `-sSTACK_SIZE=1MB`).

## 5. Avoid Dynamic Linking if Possible

Emscripten works best with static linking and static archive libraries (`.a`).
Shared libraries (`.so`, `.dylib`, `.dll`) and dynamic linking (`-sMAIN_MODULE`
/ `-sSIDE_MODULE`) add code-size and runtime overhead and should be avoided
unless runtime plugin loading is strictly required.

## 6. Porting Existing C/C++ Libraries and Build Integration

When integrating C/C++ compilation into a web application project, wire the
`emcc` / `em++` build into the project's build pipeline (such as the `"build"`
script in `package.json`) so that building the project compiles the WebAssembly
artifacts before bundling.

When building third-party C/C++ libraries with existing build systems:

### CMake Projects

Wrap `cmake` and `make` with `emcmake` and `emmake`:

```bash
mkdir -p build && cd build
emcmake cmake .. -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
emmake make
```

### Autoconf / Make Projects

Use `emconfigure` to configure cross-compilation toolchain targets and disable
shared libraries:

```bash
emconfigure ./configure --host=wasm32-unknown-emscripten --disable-shared
emmake make
```

# WebMCP

WebMCP is a browser-native JavaScript API that allows web pages to expose their client-side functionality as structured "tools" to AI agents, browser assistants, and assistive technologies. 

IMPORTANT: WebMCP is currently in Early Preview on Chromium-based browsers (such as Chrome and Edge). It requires Chromium version `146.0.7672.0` or higher and the `#enable-webmcp-testing` flag.

**Crucial Distinction:** WebMCP runs entirely **client-side** in the browser tab. It is *not* a backend server, and it does *not* use HTTP, Server-Sent Events (SSE), or `stdio` transports. The web page itself acts as the tool registry.

Currently, WebMCP **only supports Tools**. It does not support the "Resources" or "Prompts" primitives found in the backend Model Context Protocol.

## Quick Overview

- **Imperative API**: Use `document.modelContext.registerTool()` for complex logic and dynamic interactions.
- **Declarative API**: Annotate standard HTML `<form>` elements with `toolname` and `tooldescription` to turn them into tools.
- **Frameworks (MANDATORY)**: React uses `useWebMCP` from `use-webmcp-tool`. Angular uses `provideExperimentalWebMcpTools` / `declareExperimentalWebMcpTool` from `@angular/core`. Vue uses `useWebMCP` from `@vueuse/core`. **DO NOT** call `registerTool()` from components.

## Best Practices

* **Naming and Semantics**: Use specific verbs describing exact behavior (e.g. `create-event` vs `start-event-creation-process`). Favor positive descriptions over listing limitations.
* **Descriptions**: Say what the tool does and when to use it. Do not repeat parameter names, types, enum values, defaults, or limits: the agent already receives them in the input schema (your `inputSchema`, or the one the browser builds from a form's controls). Put those details in the schema, and explain a non-obvious value in that parameter's own description.
* **Schema Design**: Accept raw user input (avoid agent math/calculation). Ensure all parameters have specific types and explain the purpose of options.
* **Reliability**: Validate constraints in code and return descriptive errors for retries. Handle rate limiting gracefully. Ensure the function returns *after* UI state updates for consistency.
* **Tool Strategy**: Tools should be atomic, composable, and distinct. Do not force flow control instructions ("Don't call B after A") — let the agent decide. Register/unregister tools dynamically depending on the current page context. Use `annotations: { readOnlyHint: true }` (placed after `execute`) for tools that do not modify state to inform the agent of safe execution.
* **Clean Up**: Always use `AbortSignal` to unregister tools when pages transition or resources are released to avoid leaks and collisions. Do not use `unregisterTool`.
* **Web Development Best Practices**: WebMCP tools run as client-side JavaScript in the browser tab. They must adhere to regular web development best practices (e.g., keeping secrets out of client-side code, accessing backend databases through secure API layers, and using Web Workers, WASM, or WebGPU for heavy compute).

### When to Discourage WebMCP
* **High-Risk Actions without Guardrails**: Avoid auto-submitting tools for destructive or irreversible actions (e.g., deleting data) unless the UI requires manual user confirmation outside the agent's control.
* **Hyper-Dynamic State**: If data changes faster than the agent can react, it may work with stale context.

### Anti-Patterns & Warnings (DO NOT DO THIS)

* **Do not use backend transports.** WebMCP is for browser tabs, not Node.js background processes.
* **Do not include Resources or Prompts.** These are not supported in the current WebMCP spec.
* **Do not ignore `inputSchema` structure.** Always provide clear descriptions for every parameter to minimize agent hallucinations.
* **Do not use outside of a Secure Context (HTTPS).**

## Implementation Status

WebMCP is currently in early preview in Chromium-based browsers (e.g., Chrome, Edge):

* **Current Status**: Early preview.
* **Required Version**: Chromium `146.0.7672.0` or higher.
* **Activation**: Requires enabling the flag `chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing` or `edge://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing`.
* **Specification**: Evolving [Draft Community Group specification](https://webmachinelearning.github.io/webmcp/); not yet a standards-track recommendation.
